The code imports torch and torch.nn as nn, and builds the network inside **nn.Sequential**, which means a sequence of layers, one after another. Each layer is an **nn.Linear**, which says how many numbers it takes in and how many it gives out.
children: The first layer says that it takes two inputs and makes three outputs, the next takes three and makes two, the next takes two and makes four, and the last takes four and makes five, one per vowel.
Each layer's output size has to match the next layer's input size, so the numbers can flow through.

teaching.text: **bias=False** removes the bias, an extra constant added to a neuron's sum, so each layer only multiplies and adds, matching the diagram.
children: This code is a declaration only, with no training. It describes the network the way the machine sees it, without feeding in formants or changing any weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: **A neural network is a numerical processing machine.** It takes in numbers, processes them and makes a decision, and this one is a very simple speech recognizer that takes the formants measured from vowels in lab and decides which vowel was spoken. The two input neurons just take information from the environment, one taking F1 and the other taking F2. The five output neurons stand for done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.
children: Between them are three hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, called hidden because they are neither the input nor the output.

teaching.text: **The weights are the network's knowledge.** Every connection between two neurons has a weight, a positive or negative number, and everything the network knows about vowels is stored in these numbers.
children: The network is fully connected, so every neuron sends a connection to every neuron in the next layer, which makes 40 weights in all.
A positive weight pushes the next neuron up and a negative weight pushes it down, and the bigger the weight, the stronger the push.
The weights leaving the formants are tiny, because formants are big numbers in the hundreds and thousands of hertz, so tiny weights turn them into modest values for the rest of the network.

teaching.text: **How many layers and neurons a network should have is not known in advance.** With no hidden layers at all, the network would most likely keep making mistakes. More numbers give it more freedom, so as those numbers improve, the network can capture something as hard as recognizing a vowel from just two numbers.
children: In practice, people try the simplest design first, see how it performs, and add more.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** is how the network makes a decision, sending the input forward through the layers one at a time. The example input is F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000, there are no extra constants added in, and each hidden neuron passes its sum straight on. **Each neuron computes an inner product**, multiplying each incoming number by the weight on that connection and adding the results.
children: For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, F1 is multiplied by a small positive weight and F2 by a small negative weight. The F1 part adds a little and the F2 part takes away a bit more, so the neuron's activation lands just below zero.
None of these calculations ever have to be done by hand. What matters is understanding what is happening.

teaching.text: **The same thing repeats at every layer.** The activations of one layer become the inputs to the next, which does more inner products with its own weights, until the network reaches the output.
children: Each layer has to wait for the one before it, so a change at the input ripples all the way through.

teaching.text: **Knowledge has been reduced to positive and negative numbers, and making a decision uses nothing but multiplying and adding**, arithmetic from second grade. **Inference** means figuring out a decision, and almost all of its work is done by simple numbers that hold the knowledge and by addition and multiplication.
children: This did not come out of nowhere, since the brain's own chemistry also performs operations like addition and multiplication.

teaching.text: After the last layer, the final numbers are turned into a **probability distribution**, a set of numbers that add up to 1, and those numbers are the network's decision. The operation that does this is called **softmax**, and it just converts numbers into probabilities, so a bigger score always ends up as a bigger probability.
children: Probabilities go from 0 to 1 and percentages go from 0 to 100, but they are the same idea. A value of 0.1 means a 10 percent chance that the formants were for that vowel.
For 320 and 2000, the network gives done about 56 percent, much higher than any other vowel, so the network decides it heard done.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **This network is stupid, and all neural networks start out stupid**, because they start with random weights, which means they know nothing. This one decided done, but the formants 320 and 2000 were actually for /i/, as in dean. **A network becomes smarter only by being told the right answer**, which is given as the **desired output**.
children: The desired output for dean is zero, zero, one, zero, zero, which says there is no chance it was done, dune, Don or Dan and a 100 percent chance it was dean.
A target written with zeros and a single one is called a **one-hot encoding**.
In practice, the network gets a table of data, where each row says that when a person produced these two formants, the vowel was a particular one.

teaching.text: The output the network actually produced is the **computed output**, and the gap between it and the desired output is the **error**. Here the network gave dean only about 8 percent when it should have given it 100 percent, so the error is large. **Backpropagation** is the algorithm that changes all the weights so the network becomes a little smarter.
children: The goal is to pump up the probability of the right answer toward 1 and push the wrong ones down toward 0.
Learning is gradual, just like stochastic gradient descent. The network sees one example, changes its weights a little, sees another and changes them a little more.

teaching.text: The new weights are worked out **from the output backward**. First the connections into the outputs change, then the ones into the third hidden layer, then the second and then the first, while the activations from the forward pass stay as they were.
children: The weight from the positive neuron into dean gets bigger, which adds more to dean.
The weight from that same neuron into done gets smaller, which takes away from done.
The weights leaving the formants barely change, because they use a much smaller step size to match the large hertz values.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For any weight, the question is the same. **If this weight goes up, will the error go up or down?** Two marked weights make the comparison.

**The weight from the last hidden layer to done is an easy problem.** Done's large probability comes from an inner product that includes this weight times a positive activation of about 1.57. If the weight went up, that contribution would grow, done's probability would go up, and the network would get more wrong, since done should be zero.
children: So the weight should go down, because a smaller weight shrinks that contribution and pulls done's probability down.
There is only one inner product between this weight and the probability, so the decision is crystal clear.

teaching.text: **The weight from F1 to the first hidden layer is a hard problem.** Changing it changes the activation of its first-layer neuron, which changes the second layer, which changes the third layer, which finally changes the probabilities.
children: At every step, that change mixes with many other weights and activations, some pushing one way and some the other.
Its effect on the decision is mediated by all the intermediate calculations, so just looking at it, there is no way to tell whether it should go up or down. Backpropagation still works it out.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Why the weights are changed from the end backward is guaranteed to be on the exam.** The answer comes from comparing the last weights, labeled **W5**, with the first weights, labeled **W2**. **Improving W5 is easy**, because the output probabilities are directly determined by the last weights, and the error is very directly determined by them, so the error can be used right away to decide how to change them.

**Improving W2 is a much harder problem.** W2 affects its activations, which affect another two layers of activations along with other weights, so it is really hard to figure out how much blame W2 deserves for mistakes made all the way at the end.
children: Moreover, the effect of W2 on the errors includes the effect of W5, since W5 is downstream of W2, so any change in W2 has to pass through W5 to reach the output.

A strong exam answer explains that changing an early weight's influence on the probabilities is a much more involved, mediated set of calculations, while changing a last weight changes the probabilities right away. The last weights pose a simple, trivial problem, and the early weights pose a complex, big problem that already includes the effect of the later ones.

teaching.text: **When a problem contains smaller and smaller problems, the algorithm to use is dynamic programming.** Dynamic programming solves the easiest problem first and then uses its answer to solve the next bigger one, and it comes from Richard Bellman and Viterbi at USC.
children: So **backpropagation is SGD plus dynamic programming**. SGD changes each weight gradually, a little at a time, and dynamic programming gives backpropagation its back, since it improves the last weights first and works toward the first.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To train the network, it has to be told **the desired output for every input**, and that information is given as **two matrices**, which are just tables of numbers. Both come from the class's own lab data, with about 110 rows, one for each recording.
children: The input matrix has two columns, because the network takes two numbers in, F1 and F2.
The target matrix has five columns, because the network decides among five vowels, and each row is a one-hot answer with a one for the true vowel.

teaching.text: **The rows must line up**, because row by row the two tables describe the same recording. If the first row of formants is 500 and 1500, the first row of the target says done, and the third row, 320 and 2000, is marked dean.
children: If one table were reordered and not the other, the network would learn from the wrong answers.
The target itself never changes. Training compares the network's computed output with it and changes only the weights.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python program** trains this network, and it never has to be written from scratch, since brackets and punctuation do not matter. What matters is what each line does. **The import lines bring in a library**, which is code that someone else already wrote, so a network can be described in just a few lines.
children: Import torch means use the PyTorch library, and the second import brings in its neural network tools. These lines import into Python everything needed for doing inner products and backpropagation.
The load lines read the two saved tables from files, the same way a file is loaded when it is double-clicked.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers**, one layer after another, which is every network built so far. **nn.Linear means a layer that does inner products**, multiplying and adding.
children: The first linear layer takes two inputs and produces three outputs, the next takes three and produces two, then two to four, and finally four to five.
The network has five layers but only four linear lines, because the input layer does no processing and just receives numbers.

teaching.text: The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning. **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, here with a learning rate of 0.1, **loss** is the mistake, the gap between the computed and desired outputs, **backward** is backpropagation, and **step** actually changes the weights.
children: The program runs one gradient step using all the rows together, and it starts from PyTorch's own default weights, so it would not reproduce the hand-picked numbers in the diagram.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Neural networks did not come out of nowhere.** Their most basic features come from discoveries about animal brains. Neuroscientists discovered that there are neurons, so artificial networks have neurons, and they discovered that each neuron collects information from many other neurons, which is what the inner product does.

**Lord Edgar Adrian** won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for discovering that **neurons are nearly digital**, meaning they either fire or they don't fire. A real neuron's activation is basically off or on, while the vowel network's neurons have activations like minus 0.4 or 6.64 with no limit.
children: The **sigmoid** is an activation function added to copy Adrian's discovery. It takes the inner product and turns it into a number between 0 and 1.

If the inner product is large and positive, the sigmoid is near 1, and if it is large and negative, the sigmoid is basically 0. An inner product of minus 4 gives almost 0, and an inner product of 4 gives almost 1.
So the sigmoid digitizes neural processing, copying the brain chemistry that keeps real neurons close to off or on.

teaching.text: **Animal perception reflects this**, since some things that seem alike are perceived as different and some things that are very different are perceived as the same. In the steep middle of the S curve, two close inputs come out far apart, and out on the flat ends, two very different inputs come out nearly the same.
children: AI is duplicating animals' abilities. People often say AI has nothing to do with human cognition, but that is false, since a big reason it works is that it copies our own abilities using math as simple as multiplying and adding.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: The sigmoid can be added to the vowel network **one hidden neuron at a time**, keeping the same input and every weight the same. Each hidden neuron switches from linear to sigmoid in layer order, and the outputs still go through softmax, so they stay probabilities that add up to 1.
children: The first neuron to switch has an inner product just below zero, on the steep middle of the curve, so the sigmoid turns it into just under one half. The neuron now sends a positive number where it used to send a negative one.

teaching.text: **After each switch, everything after it is recalculated**, because later neurons get their inputs from earlier ones. So the old linear numbers cannot simply be run through the sigmoid one at a time, since each new value has to come from the updated layer before it.

As the neurons switch, **the network's answer moves**. At first it decides done with a clear majority, then done's lead shrinks until done and Don are nearly tied, then Don takes the lead, and then Dan does.
children: With all nine hidden neurons on sigmoid, Dan is on top at about 32 percent, dean has risen to about 23 percent, and done has dropped to about 16 percent.
Only the activation rule changed and no weight moved, so this is not learning. The decision changed completely, but dean still is not the top answer.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program becomes a sigmoid network by adding **nn.Sigmoid** after each hidden layer, and nn.Sigmoid means apply the sigmoid, which makes the neurons digital. The sigmoid changes the values but not how many there are, so a layer that produces three numbers still produces three, and the network keeps its 2, 3, 2, 4 and 5 shape.
children: The last linear layer has no sigmoid after it, because its five outputs go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
The sigmoid squeezes each hidden neuron on its own toward off or on, while softmax turns all five final scores together into a decision that adds up to 1.
In lab, the sigmoid can also be swapped for other functions, such as one called ReLU, to discover whether they make vowel recognition better or worse.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** simulates a very simple piece of human perception. It takes the two formants, F1 and F2, of an isolated vowel and decides which vowel it is, choosing among done, dune, dean, Don and Dan. Two input neurons take in the formants, three hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons process them, and five output neurons give the decision.
children: Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so there are 40 weights in all.

teaching.text: **The weights are the network's knowledge.** Each one is a positive or negative number, so a positive weight pushes the next neuron up and a negative one pushes it down, and the bigger the weight, the stronger the push.
children: At first the weights are random, so the network does not know anything and its decisions are stupid.
The right answer is given as a probability distribution, such as zero, zero, one, zero, zero for a dean recording, meaning a 100 percent chance it was dean.
That target is usually very different from what the stupid network produces at first, and the network learns by correcting the mistake between the two.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries one input through the network to a decision. The example vowel has F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000, which is one person's /i/. **Every step is an inner product**, multiplying each incoming number by its weight and adding the results.
children: For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the F1 part adds a little and the F2 part takes away a little more, so its activation lands just below zero.
Because those two weights point in opposite directions, a higher F1 pushes this neuron up while a higher F2 pushes it down.
The other neurons do the same with their own weights, layer by layer, until the network reaches a decision.

teaching.text: The last numbers are turned into a **probability distribution**, a set of numbers that add up to 1, by an operation called **softmax**. Softmax makes every score positive and divides each by the total, so a bigger score always gives a bigger probability, and raising one vowel's score lowers the others' probabilities.
children: With these weights, done gets the highest percentage, about 56 percent, so the network decides done.
But the correct answer is dean, so the network's knowledge is wrong and it has to change its weights.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The vowel data from the class's own lab is plotted with F1 along one axis and F2 along the other, and **each vowel forms a cloud of points**, since the same vowel comes out a little differently every time. Some patterns are clear. /i/, as in dean, sits apart with a high F2 and a low F1, just as the theory predicts, and the vowel of Dan spreads toward high F1 values.

**But there is a lot of overlap.** The vowels of dune, Don and done crowd into the same region, so a new speaker whose formants land there could be any of the three. Some points are probably errors, but real data always has errors, so they stay in because that is what real life is like.
children: If every vowel sat in its own separate spot, recognizing vowels would be easy. Instead, a network has to see the data many times to learn what really separates the vowels, and no setting of the weights can separate recordings that land on top of each other.

teaching.text: This overlap was discovered once **spectrograms** became widely available, when **Peterson and Barney** measured many speakers' vowels and found this enormous overlap.
children: For about 70 years people tried to write programs to solve it, including trying to normalize away the differences between speakers, and none of it worked.
What finally worked, around 2011 or 2012, was a neural network with backpropagation.

Everyone predicted that a static problem like two formants from one moment would be easy and that moving speech would be very hard, but everyone was wrong. Large language models deal with very dynamic information and work much better.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the algorithm that changes all the weights so the network makes better decisions, and it is made of two algorithms. **Stochastic gradient descent** improves each weight gradually, the same way SGD improved an estimate of an average, and it has the same learning rate. **Dynamic programming** decides the order, so the last weights get improved first and the earlier ones after.

Comparing two outputs gives the error. The **computed output** is what the network produced, putting most of the probability on done and only about 8 percent on dean. The **desired output** is the right answer, with a one for dean and zeros everywhere else.
children: The difference between them is the **error**, or **loss**, and more probability on dean means less error.
The error says exactly how each output should move, so done's probability should go down, dean's should go up, and the others should go down.

teaching.text: **The weights are changed from the end backward.** First come the connections into the outputs, then into the third hidden layer, then the second and then the first, while the activations from the forward pass stay fixed and are reused.
children: The weight from the positive neuron into dean gets bigger, the weights from the negative neurons into dean get smaller, and the weight from the positive neuron into done gets smaller.
The weights leaving the formants barely move, because they use a much smaller step to match the large hertz values.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: Two marked weights pose the same question, namely whether raising the weight would make the error go up or down. **The weights at the end of the network are much easier to change than the weights at the beginning.**

**The end weights are easy because they directly change the decision.** Done's large probability comes from multiplying a weight of 0.1 by a positive activation of 1.57, along with the other products feeding done. If that weight went up to something like 0.5, done's probability would go up, which is the exact opposite of what is needed.
children: So that weight should go down, since any change to an end weight is directly, automatically and immediately reflected in the percentages.

teaching.text: **The beginning weights are hard because their effect is buried under many layers.** Changing a first-layer weight changes that layer's activations, which change the next layer's activations, which change the third layer, which finally change the percentages.
children: Just looking at an early weight, there is no way to tell which direction it should move. Backpropagation still figures it out.
This is the same trap as the greedy choice in dynamic programming, where picking the cheaper of two next steps without looking ahead can lead to the wrong answer.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming says that if problems can be ordered by difficulty, solve the easiest first, then the next, and so on to the hardest.** Backpropagation follows exactly that order. The last weights are the easiest problem, because the output probabilities and the error are directly determined by them, so the error can be used right away.
children: The first weights are the hardest problem, because they affect their activations, which affect another two layers of activations along with other weights, and their effect on the error already includes the effect of the later weights.

teaching.text: **Solving the end first makes the rest easier.** Changing the last weights first teaches something that makes the next layer's problem easier, and that makes the layer after it easy too, all the way back to the start.
children: So backpropagation is Bellman and Viterbi dynamic programming combined with SGD, with SGD improving each weight a little at a time and dynamic programming saying to go from the end backward.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation is how every modern AI system learns.** Today's largest systems run it on trillions of weights, one small step at a time.
children: These ideas come from physics and are closely tied to the dynamical systems behind acoustics and masses and springs.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To train the network, it gets **two matrices**, which are tables of numbers with about 110 rows, one for each student recording. The input matrix holds each recording's F1 and F2, and the target matrix holds a one-hot answer for each recording.
children: Each row in one table goes with the same row in the other, so the row with 320 and 2000 is paired with dean.

teaching.text: **Learning picks rows one at a time.** It takes one row, such as 800 and 1700, uses its weights to calculate a decision, and changes its weights if that decision differs from the desired answer, starting from the last weights. Then it picks another row and does the same.
children: **If the network already gets a row right, there is no error, so there is nothing to learn from that row.** That can be a serious problem, since a network can get rows right by accident over and over and stop learning before it learns the real pattern.

teaching.text: **Children learning English go through the same problem**, as Carol Chomsky discovered in the early 1960s. At first, very young children say go and went correctly, because they are just memorizing what they hear.
children: Then they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs add ed for the past, as in jump and jumped, and they start saying goed.

Only later do they learn that some verbs are exceptions and get both the regular and the exceptional verbs right. Neural networks also can just memorize weights that give the right answers without learning the pattern, which is what makes learning so difficult.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python program** builds and trains the network, and it never has to be written from scratch, since brackets and dots do not matter. **The import lines bring in libraries**, collections of programs that other people wrote for one job, which can be used without knowing how they work inside.
children: Before libraries like PyTorch existed, everyone doing AI had to write their own backpropagation code.
The import lines import into Python everything for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work, which is why the whole training program fits on one page.

teaching.text: **Sequential means a neural network that is a sequence of layers.** All the networks built so far are a sequence of layers, while a large language model is a network that is not just a sequence of layers. **Each Linear line is one processing layer**, a layer that has weights and does inner products with the incoming information.
children: The first linear line says it receives information from two neurons and has three neurons, and the following lines go from three to two, two to four, and four to five.
The network has five layers but only four lines, because the input layer does no processing.

teaching.text: **The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning.** SGD is stochastic gradient descent and lr is the learning rate, here 0.1. **A bigger learning rate learns a lot faster but is less accurate, while a smaller one is more accurate but learns much slower.**
children: Loss is the mistake, so the network calculates its mistakes and learns from them, and backward is backpropagation.
Nothing changes until step is called, which is when the weights actually change.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Neural networks do not come out of nowhere.** Their basic features come from discoveries about animal brains, since scientists found that brains have neurons and that each neuron collects information from many other neurons, which is the inner product. **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for discovering that **neurons are nearly digital**, meaning they either fire or they don't fire.
children: A real neuron's activation is off or on rather than any number, while the vowel network's neurons have activations like minus 0.4, 6.64 and 1.57.

teaching.text: **The sigmoid** is an activation function added to networks to copy Adrian's discovery. It takes a neuron's linear activation, its inner product, and turns it into a number between 0 and 1.
children: If the inner product is large and positive the sigmoid is near 1, and if it is large and negative the sigmoid is basically 0, so minus 4, minus 6 or minus 1000 all give almost 0, while 4, 6 or 100 all give almost 1.
So the sigmoid digitizes neural processing, copying the brain chemistry that keeps real neurons close to off or on.

teaching.text: Near zero the curve is steep, so a small change in the inner product makes a big change in the output, while far from zero it is flat, so even big changes barely matter. **Animal perception reflects this**, since some things that seem alike are perceived as different and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.
children: AI is duplicating animals' abilities. People will say AI has nothing to do with human cognition, but that is false, and a big reason it works is that it copies our own abilities.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: The sigmoid is added **one hidden neuron at a time**, while the input and every weight stay the same. The first neuron to switch has an inner product just below zero, on the steep middle of the curve, so it comes out just under one half and now sends a positive number instead of a negative one.
children: After each switch, everything downstream is recalculated, because later neurons depend on earlier ones.
So the sigmoid network cannot be made by running the old linear numbers through the sigmoid one at a time.

teaching.text: With all nine hidden neurons on sigmoid, every hidden activation sits between 0 and 1, and **Dan becomes the top answer**, at about 32 percent, while dean rises to about 23 percent and done drops to about 16 percent.
children: Only the activation rule changed and no weight moved, so this is not learning.
The decision changed completely, but dean is still not the top answer.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each of the first three linear layers, and it means apply the sigmoid, which makes the neurons digital. The layer sizes stay 2, 3, 2, 4 and 5, because the sigmoid changes values, not how many there are.
children: The last linear layer has no sigmoid, because its five scores go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
The sigmoid squeezes each hidden neuron on its own, while softmax turns all five final scores together into a decision that adds up to 1.
The training lines and the learning rate of 0.1 stay the same.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: Training runs **thousands of times**, much more than the few dozen steps needed to average a list of numbers. Each full pass of learning is called an **epoch**, and this run uses 2000 epochs, starting from random weights.
children: After every epoch, accuracy is measured without training, with the vowel that gets the largest score counted as the network's answer. Accuracy is the percentage of recordings it gets right, and these are the same recordings it learns from.

teaching.text: **Accuracy starts at 20 percent, which is chance.** At the start the weights are random, so the network knows nothing, but it still is not at zero, because with five vowels a random guess is right one time in five.
children: Chance means how often someone would be right just by guessing randomly, so with five possible answers chance is 20 percent.

teaching.text: **After about 200 epochs, accuracy jumps up into the 40s**, so the network is learning something. It dips back toward chance for a moment, recovers, and then levels off at about 45 percent after a few hundred epochs.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: The same training is run **ten times**, each time starting from different random weights, and everything else is identical. All ten start near 20 percent, some leave chance quickly and others stay flat longer, and several briefly drop back toward chance. After a few hundred epochs they come together, and **all ten finish at the same accuracy, about 45 percent**.
children: **Different starting weights change the path, not the destination**, because the learning process is so similar each time.

teaching.text: **The network levels off well below 100 percent because the data overlap so much.** About 45 percent is clearly better than chance, so the network has learned something, but it is still pretty low, because AI is not magic.
children: If a person had to name the vowel for formants landing where several vowels overlap, they would have to squint hard and might still guess wrong. If the decision is very hard for humans, it is not surprising that it is hard for machines.
The limit comes from two formants not being enough to separate dune, Don and done, not from unlucky starting weights, so trying more starting points would not help.

In lab, different designs can be tested by adding or removing layers, changing the number of neurons, or swapping in the sigmoid or other functions, to discover whether each change improves that accuracy or makes it worse.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes in information about one moment, uses its weights to process it, and makes a decision, and it learns those weights by making errors and correcting them through backpropagation. The idea began in 1943 with a paper by **McCulloch and Pitts**, which proposed that simple mathematics could model how the brain works.
children: The paper starts from the **all-or-none** character of nervous activity, where all means active and none means inactive, so a neuron is either firing or not.
That is the same idea as the sigmoid, so the very first paper on artificial neural networks starts from biology about how real neurons behave.

teaching.text: By 1986, the ideas had matured into the two **Parallel Distributed Processing** books. **Parallel** means many neurons compute their activations at the same time, and **distributed** means the information from F1 and F2 is spread across all the neurons.
children: By then forward propagation and backpropagation were well formed.

teaching.text: **Given some static vector of formants, these networks could make a decision about a few possible categories.** A vector is just a list of numbers, and static means one fixed list from one moment. But **human cognition is far more complex** than taking in one list of numbers and giving one decision at the end.
children: Speech is incredibly time-varying, because every little moment in time gives a new formant.
Language is time-varying too, since a sentence is a whole bunch of words, one after another.
Giving a network one bunch of numbers can never model cognition that unfolds in time.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: In 1985, **Michael Jordan** developed **recurrent neural networks** to make sense of **speech production**, meaning how the tongue, velum and lips move over time. He realized that a regular neural network could never handle something that complex and time-varying, so he designed a new kind of network, and that line of work became large language models and then agentic AI. The technology at the center of modern AI was born from thinking about speech.
children: His network is not just sequential, one layer after another, because it has two layers working in parallel.
Plan units say what sequence to produce, hidden units combine information, output units give the response, and the new state units hold what the network has just produced.

teaching.text: **The network is called recurrent because it takes its output and sends it back into part of its input.** It produces something at one moment, that output loops back into the state units, and the network uses it to predict the next moment, and then the moment after that.
children: In the measured performance on a sequence of speech sounds, the rounding feature rises early and stays high across many sounds, because outputs fed back from one moment carry into the next.
GPT works the same way one word at a time. It predicts the next word, feeds the prompt plus that word back in, predicts the next word again, and keeps going.

teaching.text: Each idea grew out of earlier ones. Simple model neurons were refined into the networks of the 1980s, and Jordan's recurrent network was refined over many years into today's large language models.
children: Following that chain of ideas matters far more than remembering any of the years.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: AI systems build up in steps, and **each step extends the one before it**. **A single neuron takes in a list of numbers and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds them all up, which is the inner product, and the symbol sigma just means add them up.
children: This uses nothing but second-grade multiplication and addition to model the electrochemical activity of a real neuron, and a profound idea can start out that simple.

teaching.text: **A neural network takes in one list of numbers and gives back a whole list of decisions.** Its layers are linked by sets of weights, and each set turns one list of numbers into the next through many inner products, until the last layer gives one value for each possible answer.
children: The vowel network is this kind of network, and it still takes only one list of numbers.

teaching.text: **A large language model takes in many lists of numbers, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision about what comes next.** Here it takes 15 vectors, each standing for something at one moment in time, such as one word of a sentence, and its job is to predict the sixteenth.
children: In real systems there can be up to a million of these vectors, and that set is called the **context window**.
The sixteenth vector is a probability distribution over the next word, giving the likelihood that each word comes next.

teaching.text: **A large language model is made of neural networks**, since each block of weights is a layer, and real systems have hundreds of layers. The knowledge is still in the weights, so an LLM's knowledge of how to write an essay is stored in its weights.
children: An LLM is also a **dynamical system**. A mass-spring system starts from initial conditions and the system decides what happens next, and an LLM's initial condition is its set of input vectors, which each layer turns into better vectors until the last layer can predict the next word.
The calculation at every step is the inner product, multiplying and adding billions or trillions of times.

teaching.text: **An LLM learns by predicting the next word and correcting its mistakes.** Given the cat sat on the, with mat as the real next word, a new LLM with random weights predicts something silly like in, and backpropagation adjusts its trillions of weights so the prediction moves toward mat.
children: Repeating this with about a trillion sentences, the system surprisingly ends up knowing how to speak English.
The first problem LLMs solved was machine translation, and the same design then worked for speech and many other problems.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a graph of LLMs**, and an agent in AI today is just an LLM. One LLM outlines the answer, another writes it out in smooth sentences, a **critic** LLM criticizes the draft, a revision LLM sends it back to the critic if it is not good enough, and a final LLM produces the output.
children: The critic is what fixed **hallucination**, the system making things up, and the back-and-forth is why many systems take a while to respond.
Neurons make neural networks, neural networks make LLMs, and LLMs make agentic systems, much as molecules make cells and cells make organs.

teaching.text: **The chief insight behind all of this is Gestalt completion.** People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though none is drawn, and training a system only to predict the missing thing turns out to emulate human cognition.
children: Underneath everything, **inference is inner products**, and **learning is SGD plus dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: **An LLM takes 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth**, and since a vector is just a list of numbers, those numbers can stand for almost anything. Whatever they stand for, the machine plays the same game of predicting the next one.

The vectors can be **words**. In the cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the blank, the sixteenth vector is the missing next word, and a speaker of English knows a likely completion, such as branch or mat.
children: Getting it right means using the whole sentence, since it was the cat, not the dog, that sat.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **slices of sound**. A spectrogram is cut into little frames, each frame becomes one vector of frequencies and amplitudes, and the system learns to predict the next little piece of speech from all the previous pieces.
children: This gave the best speech recognition in 75 years, and it is also the basis for synthetic voices that are now very hard to tell from humans.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **pieces of a picture**. A picture is cut into 16 patches read row by row, and the system predicts the missing patch, which across huge numbers of pictures teaches it what a dog, a dolphin or a boat is.
children: This became the basis of modern computer vision.

teaching.text: The vectors can even be **amino acids**. A protein is a string of amino acids, which come in 20 kinds, and treating a protein as just a sequence and playing the same predict-the-next game pushed the problem of how proteins fold many years ahead.
**The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all reach it the same way, so one machine asks one question, what comes sixteenth, using the same architecture every time.
children: Because these systems predict from past data, something new that the past data does not cover can make them hallucinate.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English allows only **certain sequences of sounds** in its words, and knowing which sequences are allowed is called **phonotactic knowledge**. **A simple syllable in English can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, mat, sit, cup, dog and fish.
children: The pattern is about sounds, not letters, so the silent e in shave, kite and rope does not count, and two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, chin and bath.

teaching.text: Syllables can also have **clusters**, groups of consonants together. A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat and black, and a cluster after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help and lamp.
children: Each real word has an impossible twin marked with a star, and many twins use the same letters in the other order, such as flat and lfat, help and hepl, and lamp and lapm, so order matters.

**The order mirrors around the vowel.** In flat the l sits right next to the vowel with the f farther out, and in help the l again sits next to the vowel, now on the other side, with the p farther out. Each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant against the vowel.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables**, such as ba-na-na, At-lan-tic and ath-lete. The sounds t and l are fine across a syllable break, but tl cannot start a syllable, which is why Atlantic is a word but tlantic is impossible.
children: The sound ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one.
So whether a sequence of sounds is allowed depends on where the syllable breaks fall.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Phonotactic knowledge can be revealed through GPT learning.** Each item is the start of an English word, and the task is to guess the next letter. People agree on their guesses quickly, and how much they agree changes from item to item.
**After a vowel, almost anything can follow.** After ra, likely letters include t, n, r and l, and many others are possible too, because once a vowel has come the onset is over.
children: **At the start of a word, the choices narrow sharply** to exactly what an English onset allows. After sp the next letter is l, r or a vowel and never n, and after k it is a vowel or n, as in knee.
After b and f it is r, l or a vowel, after sh it is a vowel or r, as in shrimp, and after skr or m at the start of a word only a vowel can come.
After bram, the letter b is almost forced, as in bramble, though a new syllable could also start there.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item**, the same next-token game an LLM plays. A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, because its predictions can only get good by matching the patterns of English syllables.
children: Its prediction is a probability distribution over the next letter, and the shape of that distribution carries the knowledge.
After fa the distribution is flat, spread over many letters, while after skr it is sharply peaked on a few vowels, because English allows nothing else there.
The more the letters so far restrict what can come next, the more the probability piles onto a few letters.
